name: Renuka Devi Temple, Mahur (Ekaveera)
deity: Goddess Renuka, worshipped as Ekaveerika (Mahurye Ekaveera), mother of Parashurama
period: Ancient Shakta seat on the Mahurgad hill; the present temple is traditionally attributed to the Yadavas of Devagiri (12th to 13th century)
summary: On the hill of Mahurgad in Nanded district, the Renuka Devi temple is the seat of Ekaveerika named in the Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram, where Renuka, the mother of Parashurama, is worshipped as a self-manifested goddess.

sections.history: Mahur, also called Mahurgad, lies among the hills of Nanded district in Maharashtra, an old sacred and strategic hill site whose fort passed through many hands over the centuries. Three hilltops are held sacred here: one bears the Renuka temple, the highest carries the shrine of Dattatreya, and a third honours Anasuya, his mother. The Renuka temple is commonly attributed to the Yadavas of Devagiri and dated to the twelfth or thirteenth century, though sources differ and the seat itself is far older in tradition. The Ashtadasha Shakti Peetha Stotram attributed to Adi Shankaracharya names the Goddess here as Ekaveerika, in the line Mahurye Ekaveerika, and the temple is counted among the three and a half Shakti Peethas of Maharashtra. Traditions differ on which part of Sati's body fell here: the right arm is often named, while local belief also speaks of the head of Mother Renuka. The temple authorities hold that Adi Shankaracharya himself came here on pilgrimage.
sections.architecture: The Renuka temple crowns a hill about two kilometres from Mahur village, and the approach rises by stairs and gateways towards a wide view of the forested hills. The goddess is worshipped as a swayambhu, a self-manifested form of which only the head and face are seen above the ground, dressed for worship in cloth, garlands and ornaments. The hill-fort around the village was raised in dark basalt, and its great Hathi Darwaja gateway and the Injala or Brahmatirth tank set between the hills are still shown to visitors. On the highest hill the shrine of Dattatreya is unusual in holding a full image of the deity rather than only his sacred footprints.
sections.legends: Renuka was the wife of the sage Jamadagni and the mother of Parashurama, remembered for her steadfast devotion. In the best known telling, her husband's anger fell upon her, and Parashurama, obeying his father's word, severed her head; he then asked for her life as his boon and she was restored, her bond with her son unbroken. Local tradition holds that her head fell on the hill of Mahur, where she is still worshipped as the Mother who suffered and was made whole. Mahur is equally honoured as the birthplace of Dattatreya, born to the sage Atri and the devoted Anasuya, so that here the Mother's seat and the son of the ascetics stand on neighbouring hills. Behind all such places lies the Shakti Peetha story: when Sati gave up her life at her father Daksha's sacrifice, grief-stricken Shiva carried her body across the land, and wherever its parts fell a seat of the Goddess arose.
sections.festivals: Sharadiya Navaratri is the great season at Mahur. It opens with the ritual installation of the sacred pot, Ghatasthapana, and the nine nights are kept with daily worship, lamps and large gatherings of pilgrims. On Vijayadashami, the day of Dasara, a very large fair is held in honour of Renuka Devi. Devotees of Dattatreya also keep his festivals on the neighbouring hill. Confirm dates locally, as they follow the lunar calendar.
sections.experience: Mahur rewards those who come with time. The way to the goddess rises through a quiet hill town and then by stairs, with the forested ridges of the Deccan opening around you. At the top the darshan is simple and close: the face of the self-manifested Mother, whom pilgrims from Maharashtra and neighbouring states approach with great tenderness. Many continue to the shrine of Dattatreya on the highest hill and to the temple of Anasuya, making the day a small circuit of three sacred hilltops. Start early, carry water, and expect large crowds at Navaratri and Dasara.

visit.timings: Typically open from about 6 AM to 9 PM, with a pause for rituals; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected: dhotis or trousers for men, sarees, salwar kameez, or long skirts for women, with shoulders and knees covered. Footwear is left at the base of the steps or at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally not allowed inside the inner sanctum. Follow the notices displayed at the temple and ask the staff before photographing rituals or priests.
visit.gettingThere: Mahur lies in the far north-east of Nanded district, about 125 to 130 km from Nanded, which has the nearest major railway station and airport; Kinwat, about 50 km away, is a nearer railhead. State buses run to Mahur from the Nanded bus stand. The temple stands on a hill about 2 km from Mahur village, reached by road and then by steps.
